To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the attentional process of summation is similar for both intra- and inter-dimensional composite-stimulus stimuli.

the same processes that control the discrimination of interdimensional composite stimuli (i.e., the discrimination of the components of a compound stimulus that vary in different stimulus dimensions) also control the discrimination of intradimensional composite (compound) stimuli.
the same processes control intradimensional and interdimensional stimulus discriminations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how animals learn to attend to and respond differentially to stimuli that vary along multiple stimulus dimensions.
how animals learn to discriminate between stimuli that vary along two or more dimensions and how these discriminations are affected by attentional processes.
the effects of attentional processes on stimulus control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

attentional summation is an important factor in discrimination learning, and that the summation of attentional processes is controlled by the same factors that control the summation of the sensory components of the stimulus.
the present study provides strong support for Weiss' (1973) summation model.
the results of this experiment provide further evidence for the generality of the additive summation principle in the control of discrimination learning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
summation is a function of the degree to which the component dimensions of the stimulus are associated with reward.
the additive summation of the components of a stimulus is determined by the degree to which the components are associated with the same reinforcement contingency.
attentional processes are not stimulus-specific and that attention can be allocated to different stimulus dimensions in an additive manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the same attentional processes control intradimensional and interdimensional discriminations.
the attentional processes that underlie discrimination learning are not specific to a particular dimension of a compound stimulus.
the same attentional processes control intradimensional and interdimensional discriminations.
